'''Benjamin Guy Davis''' (born 8 August 1970)<ref name=whoswho/> is a British chemist who is [[Professor]] of [[Chemical biology]]<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Rosalind Franklin Institute and Pharmacology announce strategic partnership in Next Generation Chemistry — Department of Pharmacology |url=https://www.pharm.ox.ac.uk/news/rosalind-franklin-institute-and-pharmacology-announce-strategic-partnership-in-next-generation-chemistry |access-date=2022-11-24 |website=www.pharm.ox.ac.uk}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=2021-12-07 |title=Franklin and Oxford Pharmacology join forces |url=https://www.harwellcampus.com/franklin-and-oxford-pharmacology-strategic-partnership/ |access-date=2022-11-24 |website=Harwell Campus |language=en-GB}}</ref> in the Department of Pharmacology and a member of the Faculty (by courtesy) in the [[Chemistry Research Laboratory, University of Oxford|Department of Chemistry]] at the [[University of Oxford]]<ref name=scopus>{{Scopus id}}</ref><ref name=rsc>{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080602083757/http://www.rsc.org/Publishing/Journals/cb/Volume/2007/2/InterviewwithBenDavis.asp|archive-date=2 June 2008|url=http://www.rsc.org/Publishing/Journals/cb/Volume/2007/2/InterviewwithBenDavis.asp|title=Interview with Ben Davis: Sugar Solutions|publisher=[[Royal Society of Chemistry]]|author=Anon|year=2007}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://users.ox.ac.uk/~dplb0149/|title=The Davis Group - Home|first=Philippe|last=Garnier|website=Users.ox.ac.uk}}</ref><ref name=epmc>{{EuropePMC|ORCID=0000-0002-5056-407X}}</ref> and a [[Fellow]] of [[Pembroke College, Oxford]].<ref name=pem>{{cite web|url=https://www.pmb.ox.ac.uk/fellows-staff/profiles/professor-ben-davis|title=Professor Ben Davis - Pembroke College|website=Pmb.ox.ac.uk|access-date=21 May 2018|archive-date=14 April 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180414060245/https://www.pmb.ox.ac.uk/fellows-staff/profiles/professor-ben-davis|url-status=dead}}</ref> He also holds the role of Science Director for Next Generation Chemistry<ref>{{Cite web |title=Science Director, Next Generation Chemistry - Professor Ben Davis |url=https://www.rfi.ac.uk/our-people/ben-davis/ |access-date=2025-05-09 |website=Rosalind Franklin Institute |language=en-GB}}</ref> (2019-) at the [[Rosalind Franklin Institute]].

==Education==
Davis was privately educated at [[Nottingham High School]]<ref name=whoswho/> followed by the [[University of Oxford]] where he was awarded [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in Chemistry (with Chemical Pharmacology) in 1993{{citation needed|date=May 2018}} and a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] in 1996 supervised by {{ill|George Fleet|qid=Q29347931}}.<ref>{{Cite web |title=George Fleet |url=https://www.chem.ox.ac.uk/people/george-fleet |access-date=2023-11-18 |website=www.chem.ox.ac.uk |language=en}}</ref><ref name=phd>{{cite thesis |degree=DPhil |first=Benjamin Guy |last=Davis |title=Synthesis of inhibitors of sugar processing enzymes |publisher=University of Oxford |date=1996 |url=https://copac.jisc.ac.uk/id/46162557?style=html |id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.711593}} |website=jisc.ac.uk |oclc=1064614676 }}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> He was a student of [[Keble College, Oxford]].<ref name=dplb0149/>

==Research and career==
Davis spent two years as a [[postdoctoral research]] [[fellow]] in the laboratory of {{ill|J. Bryan Jones|qid=Q56612499}}<ref>{{Cite web |title=Profile of J. Bryan Jones |url=https://sites.chem.utoronto.ca/chemistry/staff/JBJ/profile.htm |access-date=2023-11-18 |website=sites.chem.utoronto.ca}}</ref> at the [[University of Toronto]], exploring protein chemistry and biocatalysis.<ref name=frs>{{cite web|title=Professor Benjamin Davis FRS |publisher=[[Royal Society]] |location=London |author=Anon|year=2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151117101055/https://royalsociety.org/people/benjamin-davis-11314/ |archive-date=17 November 2015 |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/benjamin-davis-11314 }} One or more of the preceding sentences incorporates text from the royalsociety.org website where: {{blockquote|"All text published under the heading 'Biography' on Fellow profile pages is available under [[Creative Commons license|Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License]]." --{{cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/about-us/terms-conditions-policies/ |title=Royal Society Terms, conditions and policies |access-date=9 March 2016 |url-status=bot: unknown |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150925220834/https://royalsociety.org/about-us/terms-conditions-policies/ |archive-date=25 September 2015 }}}}</ref> There he developed, with Jones and Genencor International Inc., early examples of targeted protein degradation systems.<ref>{{Cite patent|number=WO2000064485A2|title=Specifically targeted catalytic antagonists and uses thereof|gdate=2000-11-02|invent1=Davis|invent2=Jones|invent3=Bott|invent4=Sanford|inventor1-first=Benjamin G.|inventor2-first=John Bryan|inventor3-first=Richard R.|inventor4-first=Karl John|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/WO2000064485A2/en}}</ref> In 1998 he returned to the United Kingdom to take up a [[lectureship]] at [[Durham University]]. In the autumn of 2001 he moved to the [[Dyson Perrins Laboratory]] in the [[Chemistry Research Laboratory, University of Oxford|Department of Chemistry]] and received a [[fellow]]ship at [[Pembroke College, Oxford]].{{citation needed|date=May 2018}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Barlow |first=John |date=2003 |title=Welcoming New Fellows, Ben Davis |url=https://issuu.com/pembrokecollegeoxford/docs/pcr_2000-2003_pt1_compressed |journal=Pembroke College Record |volume=2000-2003 |pages=19 |via=Pembroke College, Oxford}}</ref> He was promoted to Professor of Chemistry in 2005.<ref name=frs/> In 2021 in a new partnership<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> between the Rosalind Franklin Institute and the University of Oxford he took up a joint position between Medical Sciences in the Department of Pharmacology and the role of Science Director for Next Generation Chemistry. From 2020-2024 he was the Deputy Director and then the Interim Director (November 2023 to April 2024) of the Rosalind Franklin Institute.

His group's research centres on the chemical understanding and exploitation of biomolecular function ([[Synthetic Biology|synthetic biology]], [[Chemical Biology|chemical biology]] and chemical medicine), with an emphasis on carbohydrates and proteins. In particular, the group's interests encompass synthesis and methodology; target biomolecule synthesis; inhibitor/probe/substrate design; [[biocatalysis]]; enzyme and biomolecule mechanism; biosynthetic pathway determination; [[protein engineering]]; [[drug delivery]]; [[molecular biology]]; [[structural biology]]; [[cell biology]]; [[glycobiology]]; molecular imaging and ''[[in vivo]]'' biology.<ref name=frs/>

Research in the Davis laboratory has been funded by the [[Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council]], the [[Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council]], the [[Medical Research Council (United Kingdom)|Medical Research Council]], [[UCB (company)|UCB-Celltech]], [[AstraZeneca]], the [[European Union]], [[GlaxoSmithKline]], [[Cancer Research UK]], the [[Wellcome Trust]] and the [[Royal Society]].<ref name=dplb0149/> 

===Awards and honours===
Davis was elected a [[List of Fellows of the Royal Society elected in 2015|Fellow of the Royal Society in 2015]].<ref name=frs/> His certificate of election reads: {{centered pull quote|Professor Davis is noted for his chemical interrogation and manipulation of biological systems, particularly those that hinge on [[carbohydrate]]s and [[protein]]s. He has developed selective and benign bond forming strategies that have been applied to biology, allowing the construction of [[Chemical synthesis|synthetic biomolecules]] and [[Bioconjugation|bioconjugates]]; the creation of synthetic cells and viruses; and [[in vivo]] chemistry. These have enabled associated mechanistic details of protein and [[Glycobiology|sugar biology]] to be elucidated and exploited for [[biotechnology|biotechnological applications]].<ref name=royal>{{cite web |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/fellowship/2015/benjamin-davis/ |title = Professor Benjamin Davis FRS |archive-date=2 May 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150502131121/https://royalsociety.org/people/fellowship/2015/benjamin-davis/ |location=London|publisher=The Royal Society}}</ref>}}

In 2017, he was elected a Member of the [[Academia Europaea|Academia Europea]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Academy of Europe: Davis Benjamin |url=https://www.ae-info.org/ae/Member/Davis_Benjamin |access-date=2022-11-24 |website=www.ae-info.org}}</ref> and in 2019, he was elected a [[Fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=8 May 2019 |title=New Fellows: 50 top biomedical and health scientists join the Academy |url=https://acmedsci.ac.uk/more/news/new-fellows-50-top-biomedical-and-health-scientists-join-the-academy- |access-date=13 June 2019 |work=[[Academy of Medical Sciences, United Kingdom]]}}</ref>

He was also a recipient of the [[Mullard Award]] from the [[Royal Society]] in 2005, the [[Philip Leverhulme Prize]] in 2002 and the [[Meldola Medal and Prize]] in 1999 from the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]].<ref name="gongs">{{cite web|url=http://users.ox.ac.uk/~dplb0149/people/bdavis.html#Prizes|title=The Davis Group - Ben G. Davis|first=Philippe|last=Garnier|website=Users.ox.ac.uk|access-date=21 May 2018}}</ref> He won the Whistler Award<ref>{{Cite web |title=Roy L Whistler International Award in Carbohydrate Chemistry – International Carbohydrate Organisation |url=https://ico.chemistry.unimelb.edu.au/whistler-award/ |access-date=2022-11-24 |language=en-US}}</ref> of the [[International Carbohydrate Organization]] in 2016. He also received the [[Davy Medal]] ("awarded for outstanding contributions in the field of chemistry"<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Davy Medal {{!}} Royal Society |url=https://royalsociety.org/grants-schemes-awards/awards/davy-medal/ |access-date=2022-11-24 |website=royalsociety.org}}</ref>) from the [[Royal Society]] in 2020.<ref name=":2" />
